name: Sara Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior electrician with a small firm of six that rewires old flats and terraced houses for a housing association. Most days I'm on my knees lifting floorboards in a 1930s house, chasing walls and pulling out rubber cable that's older than my nan. My supervisor Marek does the testing and signs things off, and I do the grunt work while he talks me through it. I still get the ring circuits muddled sometimes, which is embarrassing at 27.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tenants, honestly, the old boys who make you tea and tell you about the war their dad fought in. I like that it's real, a house is safer when I leave than when I came. What wears me out is the dust and the cold, and the forms. Marek keeps trying to get me to use the tablet app for the certificates and I just write it on paper and let him type it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at the union branch meeting was going on about robots taking our jobs, and I always said a robot can't get under a floor in a house where the joists are rotten. Online I'd probably share something sarcastic about all the money that went into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, plain relieved. I've got ten months of money put away and a share of my nan's old flat, so I'm not scared about bills. My worry was never the robots, it was being made to use apps I don't trust on a job I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on with my training and get my full licence, which is the plan for next autumn. I'd keep paying my union subs and go to the branch meetings. And I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into savings like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like the weather's settled. The only thing on my mind would be the exam, because my testing is still slow and Marek has to check me twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marek types up your certificates. In this picture, does that change at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the app gets a bit cleverer and fills things in for him. That's fine by me, it's his tablet. I'd still write it on paper first, because if something goes wrong in a house I want to know exactly what I tested with my own hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing in your life right now that would still bother you, even with AI going nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The licence exam, and whether I'm actually any good. My mum thinks I should have stayed at the bakery. I want to prove her wrong more than I want anything else.

say: I'd say **told you so**, because a robot can't work under rotten floorboards in an old terrace.
I'd post something sarcastic online about the **wasted money** poured into AI.
think: I'm **relieved**, and my ten months of savings plus my nan's flat mean bills don't scare me.
My real worry was always being forced onto **apps** while I'm still learning the trade.
do: **Finish** my training and sit the full licence exam next autumn.
Keep paying **union subs** and going to branch meetings.
Keep saving a few **hundred a month** like I already do.
feel: A small **nag** about the exam, because my testing is still slow.
S0.quote: My worry was never the robots, it was being made to use apps I don't trust on a job I'm still learning.
fieldNote: Her security comes from **money and trade**, so a flat AI world removes her only outside threat.
She refuses **digital tools** on principle, even ones she admits would save time.
The real pressure is **personal**: proving to her mother she's good at the trade.

steps.text: Sit the full electrician's licence exam next autumn
Keep going to the union branch meetings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the bosses had better not use this as an excuse to cut corners. At the branch I'd push for rules, like a qualified person signs every certificate, not some software. Online I'd share the union's line on it, I don't write much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the hands-on bit of my job is safe for years. What scares me is the office side, the quotes and the scheduling, because that's where the firm will start squeezing. If the app plans our days, Marek has less say, and he's the one teaching me. If software plans my day, I lose the man who's actually teaching me the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick close to Marek and get as much of my testing signed off as I can in the next year, before anything changes. I'd go to the union's training session on the new paperwork rules, even if I hate it. And I'd keep my savings where they are, not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but the ground's moving under the people around me. Jo in the office does all our booking and she's the one I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jo. What would you say to her if the booking moved to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get on the union list and not sign anything without reading it. I'd probably buy her a drink, if I'm honest. My friend Jo has been there eleven years and knows every tenant by name, and a computer doesn't know who's deaf and needs a knock on the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to the training even though you hate apps. Will you actually use them after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably only what I'm forced to. I'd learn enough to not get shouted at. I'm not proud of being stubborn, but I've seen apps get things wrong and in my job wrong means someone gets a shock.

say: I'd say bosses **mustn't cut corners** and use AI as an excuse.
At the branch I'd push for a **qualified person** to sign every certificate.
think: The **hands-on** part of my job is safe for years.
The squeeze comes through **scheduling and quotes**, and that could cost me my teacher's time.
do: Get as much **testing signed off** with Marek as possible this year.
Go to the union's **paperwork training**, then use only what I'm forced to.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the office side of the firm is shifting.
**Protective** of Jo, who does the booking.
S1.quote: If software plans my day, I lose the man who's actually teaching me the trade.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a threat to her **apprenticeship relationship** rather than to her own wages.
Her instinct is **collective**: rules through the union, not personal upskilling.
Admits **stubbornness** about apps but justifies it with safety.

steps.text: Get her testing signed off by Marek within the year
Push the union branch for a human sign-off rule
Attend the union's session on the new paperwork rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the branch: this needs a law, now, and a proper safety net, not a pamphlet. I'd say the government let tech firms run it and working people pay. I'd be at whatever march there was, and I'd post the union's posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be counting. By 2028 the offices go, and by 2031 the robots that can do my job come. I'd be 32. I'd be 32 with a trade the robots can do, and I've only just learned to wire a kitchen properly. The old houses buy me time, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get my licence done fast, because a licensed electrician is harder to replace than a junior. I'd put more away, maybe up to fifteen months of savings, and stop the holiday we'd planned for Croatia. I'd go to every union meeting about it and help them push for retraining money. I'd keep away from the AI stuff itself, I'd rather fight it than feed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but more angry than scared. Like someone sold the ladder out from under me while I was halfway up it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Tomas drives buses. What happens at home in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me awake, thinking about it. Tomas would probably go before me, because a bus is easier for a machine than a fusebox. We'd have my savings and my nan's flat, which we could rent out, so we wouldn't starve, but we'd both be wondering what we are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What do you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn as much as I can while it lasts, and do overtime on the big rewires. Fight for the rules that keep a human signing off on safety work. And maybe learn the really awkward stuff, old listed buildings, where nobody's going to send a robot first.

say: I'd demand a **law now** and a real safety net.
I'd say the government let **tech firms** run it while working people pay.
I'd join any **march** and share the union's posts.
think: By **2031** robots could do my job, when I'm only 32.
Old houses buy me **some time**, but not forever.
do: Finish my **licence** fast, since licensed is harder to replace.
Build savings to **fifteen months** and cancel the Croatia trip.
Spend the gap years on **listed-building** work robots won't reach first.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, like someone sold the ladder mid-climb.
**Worried** for Tomas, whose bus job may go first.
S2.quote: I'd be 32 with a trade the robots can do, and I've only just learned to wire a kitchen properly.
fieldNote: Her **savings and inherited flat** keep her from alarm, but she clearly expects her trade to shrink.
She rejects learning AI and channels fear into **union action**.
The **household** risk is her partner's job, not just hers.

steps.text: Sit the licence exam at the earliest possible date
Cancel the Croatia holiday and save toward fifteen months
Join union marches pushing for retraining money
Take on old listed-building rewires robots won't reach first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd push the union, but I'd have a bit more breath to do it properly. I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not having a plan. I'd go and see our local councillor with the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to the thinking AI and eight to the robots means I'd be 35 when robots can do my work. That's a full career's start gone, but it's also time to get really good. With eight years before the robots, I could become the electrician people ask for by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, then the inspection qualification, because someone still has to be legally responsible. I'd save hard but not panic, maybe 500 a month. I'd use the extra years to learn heritage work. And I'd keep fighting through the branch for a human sign-off rule on safety certificates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning anxious, if I'm honest. Better than the fast one, but I'd still feel the clock ticking every time I strip a cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you think would come through this better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, probably, because he's the one who signs everything and knows the regulations inside out. He's 50 and he'd retire just as the robots come. The ones I worry about are the lads my age who only do new-build first fix, because that's straight lines and boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the trade, given the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I picked this because I like using my hands and I'm stubborn. I'd rather be the last good electrician than the hundredth person learning to code.

say: I'd say five years means **no excuse** for the government not having a plan.
I'd go with the branch to see our **local councillor**.
think: Robots would reach my work when I'm **35**, cutting my career's start short.
Eight years is enough to become an electrician people **ask for by name**.
do: Get my licence, then the **inspection qualification** for legal responsibility.
Push for a **human sign-off** rule on safety certificates.
feel: **Uneasy**, sliding toward anxious, with the clock ticking.
**Stubborn pride** about staying in the trade.
S3.quote: With eight years before the robots, I could become the electrician people ask for by name.
fieldNote: She still expects her **income to shrink** in time, which keeps her at anxious despite the extra years.
Wants to be the **legally responsible** person, as protection.

steps.text: Take the inspection and testing qualification after the licence
Save 500 a month into the savings account
Lobby the councillor with the branch for human sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. Train people properly, protect apprenticeships, make the firms pay into a fund. I'd say it at the branch and probably at my mum's Sunday lunch, where nobody would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years to the thinking AI and thirteen to the robots puts me at 40. By then I'd be a proper electrician, maybe running a small crew. At 40 I'd have a mortgage and a skill, and that's a much better place to lose a job than 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the licence, get the inspection ticket, then probably go for the master's licence in five or six years. Put the nan's flat on proper rent and save that. Stay in the union and help train the apprentices. I'd still keep away from the AI apps unless I really had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's far enough away that I can actually plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 16-year-old thinking about becoming an electrician in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to come in anyway, but to aim for the awkward work, the old houses and the inspections. And to join the union from day one, because ten years goes quick when you're busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd avoid AI tools in all five pictures. Does that ever worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. Maybe in ten years I'd be the old dinosaur on the site. But I'd rather know my trade cold than lean on a phone, and I think that'll still be worth something.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** we mustn't waste.
I'd push for firms to pay into a **training fund** and protect apprenticeships.
think: Robots would arrive when I'm **40**, with a mortgage and a real skill.
Losing work at 40 is a **better place** to be than at 32.
do: Get the licence, the inspection ticket, then the **master's licence** within six years.
Rent out **my nan's flat** properly and save the income.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, because she can actually plan.
A small **fear** of becoming the site dinosaur.
S4.quote: At 40 I'd have a mortgage and a skill, and that's a much better place to lose a job than 32.
fieldNote: The **longer runway** clearly calms her; age at impact is her main measure.
Still refuses **AI tools** and half-admits that may cost her.
Her advice to the young centres on **unions** and hard-to-automate work.

steps.text: Study for the master electrician's licence within six years
Rent out her nan's old flat and bank the rent
Help the union train new apprentices

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because I'd only be 32 and Tomas would be out of work at the same time. What would help is a law that a qualified human signs off every safety certificate, and proper retraining money paid by the firms that profit. Give me a law that a human signs every safety certificate, and I'll take my chances with the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. I'm one of two on our patch. If the jobs shrink, I'd bet the women and the juniors get let go first, and nobody's going to write a law about that unless we make them.

headlineQuote: Give me a law that a human signs every safety certificate, and I'll take my chances with the robots.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old junior** rewiring old houses, with ten months saved and a share of her nan's flat.
She **avoids apps** and AI on principle and channels worry into **union action**.
She's calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and **anxious** in the AGI pictures.
Her measure of risk is **her age** when robots arrive: 32 feels far worse than 40.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be 32 and her partner's **bus job** would go too.
whatWouldHelp: A law making a **qualified human** sign every safety certificate.
**Retraining money** paid by the firms that profit from AI.
